fields.meta_title: Tenant Screening Form: Build Yours Free | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a tenant screening form that pre-screens inquiries, collects signed consent for the report and records each decision against your criteria.
fields.h1: Build a Tenant Screening Form That Records Every Decision
fields.hero_description: A tenant screening form handles the step before the report: who gets a showing, and the renter's signed consent. Emergent builds it with a table of every applicant.
fields.features_subheading: The report comes from a screening service. Everything around it, from the first inquiry to the last notice, is a form you control.
fields.feature_1:
Pre-screen questions on every inquiry

Sends each inquiry a short questionnaire before any showing, with move-in date and monthly income among the questions. Answers that fit your criteria get a booking link.
fields.feature_2:
Signed authorization on any phone

Shows the screening disclosure, then captures the applicant's signature and the date it was signed. Each signed copy stays attached to the applicant, ready when anyone asks.
fields.feature_3:
A hand-off to your screening service

Connects to the screening service you already pay through its API and sends the signed authorization with the applicant's details. The service runs the report and returns it.
fields.feature_4:
Decisions saved with their reasons

Keeps every applicant as a row in a database you own, with the report summary, each criterion met or missed and the reason for the decision. Filter by unit or by status.
fields.feature_5:
Adverse action notices drafted

Drafts the notice when a report counts against a renter, naming the company that supplied the report and how to reach it. A person on your team reads each draft and sends it.
fields.feature_6:
Source code you can take anywhere

Exports the full app to your GitHub repo. A developer can add a second screening service or connect your property software, or you can ask for the change in a plain prompt.
fields.why_title: Why Build Tenant Screening With Emergent?
fields.why_description: A PDF consent page ends at the signature line. Here the signed copy reaches your screening service, and each decision keeps its reason.

fields.tab_content_1:
Showing links only for renters that fit the listing

Marcus rents a two-bedroom at 88 Birch Lane, with too many inquiries to show it to all of them. Each inquiry gets five pre-screen questions, starting with the move-in date. Answers that fit his posted criteria get a link to book a showing. Everyone else waits in his table, with no automatic reply.
fields.tab_content_2:
Signed authorizations sent to your screening service

Harbor Lane Rentals manages 40 units and orders every report from one screening service. Each applicant reads the disclosure and signs the authorization on a phone. The signed copy then goes to that service through its API. No report is ordered until the signature is in, and the table shows who has not signed.
fields.tab_content_3:
All four criteria checked for every applicant

Linden Court Apartments posts four written criteria, income and a past landlord reference among them. Reports come back from the screening service as a summary in each applicant's row. Anyone who misses a criterion goes to the leasing manager, whose reason is saved in the file.
fields.tab_content_4:
Adverse action notices that name the screening company

A report that counts against a renter, even in part, calls for a notice. When Harbor Lane asks Jordan Lee for a co-signer after his report, the app drafts one naming the screening company. It adds his right to dispute and to a free copy within 60 days. A leasing agent reviews the draft and sends it.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Tenant Screening Form
fields.howto_description: Settle what earns an approval first. The questions and every notice follow from that list.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Write the criteria before the listing
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide what an applicant must show, such as income against rent and a verifiable rental history. Put the list in writing and post it with the listing. Applying one written list to everyone, in the order they apply, gives each decision a reason you can show.
fields.howto_step_2_des: The Fair Housing Act bars decisions based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status or disability. Cut any question that points at them, such as plans for a family. Ask how many people will live in the unit instead.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Send each inquiry five or six questions tied to your criteria, with move-in date and occupancy first. Offer a showing to renters whose answers fit. Read the others yourself before replying, since a short answer can hide a good tenant.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Show the disclosure in plain words: which screening service you use and what the report covers. Ask for a signature and the date on the same page. Order nothing until the authorization is signed, and keep each signed copy with its applicant.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Link the form to the service you already use through its API. The signed authorization and the applicant's details then reach it without retyping. Send only what the service asks for. The report summary then comes back into the applicant's row.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Record every decision with its reason
fields.howto_step_6_des: Tick off the criteria an applicant meets and choose the reason from your written list. Send anyone who falls short to one person who decides. A file that shows its reason is far easier to defend than a note that says declined.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Any denial, co-signer request or higher deposit that rests even partly on a report needs an adverse action notice. Give the screening company's name, address and phone number. Say the renter may dispute it, or request the report free of charge within 60 days.

plan.angle: The live top 10 splits between landlord checklists (AAOA, Second Nature), screening services that sell the report (Zillow, the California Apartment Association) and blank PDFs (eForms, pdfFiller, Pipefile). None of them builds the step a landlord owns: the pre-screen questions before a showing, the signed authorization the report needs, a decision recorded against written criteria, and the notice the FCRA requires when a report counts against someone. This page covers that step, field by field, and leaves the report itself to the screening service the landlord already pays.
tab_stories: A landlord with one two-bedroom sends every inquiry five pre-screen questions, and only renters whose answers fit the posted criteria get the link to book a showing.

A leasing team gets the screening service's summary back into the applicant's row and records each decision against the same four written criteria, with the reason saved.
